card.name: Gotipua
card.tagline: Acrobatic Odissi precursor performed by young male dancers dressed as women.
card.profile: Gotipua is a traditional dance form from Odisha, India, and the historic precursor to classical Odissi dance. Performed by young boys who dress as women to praise Lord Jagannath and Krishna, the art incorporates intricate gestural acting, temple-inspired postures, and complex yogic acrobatics known as bandha nrutya. Dancers begin training around age five or six and perform until adolescence, when their androgynous appearance changes. Accompanied by traditional Odissi music led by the mardala drum, Gotipua has played a central role in preserving and shaping Odisha's sacred performance arts.
card.insight: During the 16th-century decline of temple devadasis under Rama Chandra Dev, young boys in Odisha took over sacred dance traditions, styling flower-knotted hair and executing bandha yoga poses to praise Jagannath.

card.profile_long:
Origins and History
Long ago, the temples of Orissa maintained female dancers known as devadasis or mahari, who were devoted to Lord Jagannath. Relief sculptures on the stone walls of ancient temples, including the Konark Sun Temple and the Jagannath Temple in Puri, witness to this ancient tradition. With the decline of the mahari dancers around the 16th century during the reign of Rama Chandra Dev (who founded the Bhoi dynasty), young boy dancers stepped in to continue the devotional tradition. In southern Orissa, particularly in the district of Ganjam, the tradition was also called Sakhi Nacha. During the 17th and 18th centuries, Oriya poets wrote numerous lyrics on the divine love of Radha and Krishna, which became integral to the repertoire. Over time, Gotipua became a major influence on modern Odissi classical dance; renowned masters such as Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra, who hailed from the historic craft village of Raghurajpur near Puri, trained as Gotipua dancers in their youth.

How It Is Danced
Gotipua performance integrates classical Odissi postures with extreme physical flexibility and expressional acting. The movement system is built upon two core foundational stances: tribhangi, in which the body bends gracefully at three points—the head, torso, and knees—and chouka, a square-like wide stance symbolizing Lord Jagannath. Dancers execute fluid movements in the upper torso that recall gentle ocean waves. A central feature of Gotipua is Bandha Nrutya, the presentation of intricate, yogic acrobatic figures (bandha) that depict scenes from Hindu mythology. The 15th-century text Abhinaya Chandrika by Maheshwara Mahapatra documents more than 25 varieties of bandha, including poses such as Gagana, Dhurmukha, Torona, Shayana, Padmasana (lotus), Hansa (swan), Mayura (peacock), and Kandarpa Ratha (chariot of the god of love). Training begins at age five or six to build the suppleness required for these intricate shapes.

Music and Instruments
The dance is set to traditional Odissi music, with the dancers themselves singing the lyrical verses. Musical accompaniment is provided by a dedicated ensemble featuring the mardala (a two-headed drum akin to a pakhawaj and the primary percussion instrument), gini (small cymbals), harmonium, violin, and bansuri (bamboo flute), alongside one or two lead vocalists. The musical repertoire draws heavily on classical and devotional compositions, including the 12th-century Gita Govinda, using ornate poetic verses to structure the expressional items.

Costume and Setting
To transform into graceful female dancers, the young boys let their hair grow long, tying it into a knot embellished with woven flower garlands. Facial makeup features mixed white and red powder, broad kajal lines around the eyes to create an elongated look, and a round bindi on the forehead surrounded by delicate sandalwood patterns unique to each dance school. Red alta liquid is painted on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. The costume includes a brightly colored blouse decorated with shiny accents (kanchula) and an embroidered silk apron tied around the waist as a ruffle (nibibandha). Some dancers wear a traditional pattasari—a thin fabric about 4 meters (13 ft 1 in) long tied tightly with a knot at the navel—though modern tailored costumes are also used. Dancers wear beaded necklaces, bracelets, armbands, ear ornaments, painted nose motifs, and ankle bells that accentuate foot rhythms. The costume, jewellery, and ankle bells are held as sacred.

Occasions and Meaning
Gotipua is fundamentally a devotional art form performed to praise Lord Jagannath and Krishna. Performances begin with a vandana prayer—an invocation giving thanks to Mother Earth, Jagannath, one's guru, and the audience, executed with a three-step salutation (above the head for God, before the face for the guru, and at the chest for the audience). The repertoire includes Sarigama (celebrating pure technique and architectural beauty) and Abhinaya (gestural narrative dance depicting Radha-Krishna poetry through facial expressions, eye movements, and hand mudras). Gotipua remains a vital cultural feature in Odisha, celebrated annually at events like the Gotipua Dance Festival in Bhubaneswar organised by the Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra Odissi Research Centre.

sections.origins_and_history: Long ago, the temples of Orissa maintained female dancers known as devadasis or mahari, who were devoted to Lord Jagannath. Sculptures of dancers on bas-reliefs in temples across Orissa, including the Konark Sun Temple and the Jagannath Temple in Puri, demonstrate this ancient tradition. With the decline of the mahari dancers around the 16th century during the reign of Rama Chandra Dev (who founded the Bhoi dynasty), young boy dancers stepped in to continue the devotional tradition. In southern Orissa, particularly in the district of Ganjam, the dance evolved as Sakhi Nacha around the 17th century. During the 17th and 18th centuries, Oriya poets composed lyrics on the love between Radha and Krishna, which were adopted by the dancers for expressional items. Gotipua heavily influenced modern Odissi classical dance; most masters of Odissi, such as Kelucharan Mohapatra from the village of Raghurajpur near Puri, were Gotipua dancers in their youth.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Gotipua performance features classical Odissi postures combined with intense yogic acrobatics. It relies on two basic postures: tribhangi (where the body is held with bends at the head, torso, and knees) and chouka (a square-like stance symbolizing Jagannath), characterized by a fluid upper torso. Performance items begin with a vandana (invocation) featuring a three-step salutation above the head, in front of the face, and at the chest. Technical precision is showcased in Sarigama, while narrative storytelling is delivered through Abhinaya using facial expressions, eye movements, and mudra gestures. A defining feature is Bandha Nrutya, where young dancers execute intricate acrobatic yogic poses (bandha) such as Padmasana (lotus pose), Hansa (swan), Mayura (peacock), Chara Mayura (grazing peacock), Garuda (mythical eagle), Kandarpa Ratha (chariot of love), Sagadi (wheel), Nauka (boat), Kaliyadalana, and Bakasura. Boys begin training at five or six years old to achieve the necessary suppleness of limb.
sections.music_and_instruments: Gotipua is accompanied by traditional Odissi music, with the primary percussion instrument being the mardala (a two-headed drum). The musical ensemble includes gini (small cymbals), harmonium, violin, bansuri (bamboo flute), and one or two vocalists, with the dancers themselves also singing the verses. The songs feature ornate Odia poetry as well as Sanskrit texts such as the 12th-century Gita Govinda.
sections.costume_and_setting: Young male dancers transform into feminine figures by letting their hair grow, tying it in a knot woven with flower garlands, and decorating their faces with white and red powder, kajal eye lining, a round bindi, and sandalwood patterns unique to each school. Palms and soles are painted with red alta liquid. Costume pieces include a brightly colored blouse (kanchula) with shiny decorations and an embroidered silk cloth apron (nibibandha) tied at the waist. Traditional dancers wear a pattasari (a thin fabric about 4 metres long tied tightly with equal lengths and a navel knot). Beaded jewellery—necklaces, bracelets, armbands, ear ornaments, and painted nose motifs—along with ankle bells, complete the costume, which is considered sacred.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Gotipua was developed as a sacred devotional practice to praise Lord Jagannath and Krishna. Performances begin with an invocation expressing gratitude to Mother Earth, Jagannath, one's guru, and the assembled audience. In present times, Gotipua is performed at cultural events, religious festivals, and dedicated gatherings such as the annual Gotipua Dance Festival in Bhubaneswar organised by the Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra Odissi Research Centre.
sections.notable_figures: Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra, a leading master of classical Odissi dance from Raghurajpur, began his artistic life as a Gotipua dancer. Maguni Charan Das, a recipient of the Padma Shri award and the Odisha Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, was another celebrated master of the Gotipua dance.
sections.regional_variants: In southern Odisha, especially in the district of Ganjam, the tradition of boy dancers performing in female attire evolved under the name Sakhi Nacha. Raghurajpur, a historic village near Puri, is famous as a traditional center for Gotipua dance troupes.
sections.lineage: Gotipua originated as an offshoot of the ancient Mahari (devadasi) temple dance tradition following its 16th-century decline, and directly gave rise to modern Odissi classical dance.
